title: Genetics: From Genes to Genomes
description: How a gene's sequence becomes a protein, how variants and inheritance patterns behave in families and populations, and what genetic tests, genome scans, gene editing and epigenetics can and cannot show. Each lesson practises one judgement a geneticist or genetic counsellor makes.
audience: Adults who have finished Biology: Cells to Ecosystems (DNA copying, meiosis, single-gene Punnett squares, mutation and selection in outline) and are comfortable multiplying and adding chances and reading ratios. No chemistry beyond that is needed.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a coding sequence with the codon table and say what a change to it does to a protein.
You'll be able to predict gene expression from conditions and mutations in a simple regulatory circuit.
You'll be able to infer genotypes from offspring counts, recombination frequencies and pedigrees, and work out a carrier chance.
You'll be able to use Hardy-Weinberg proportions to estimate carriers and to read a departure from them.
You'll be able to choose between chance and selection for a change in allele frequency and say what evidence would decide.
You'll be able to say what a genetic test result, a genome-wide association or a polygenic score does and does not tell a person.
You'll be able to weigh a gene-editing proposal and an epigenetic claim against the evidence.

modules.title: From DNA to protein
modules.summary: What a genome holds, how a gene's sequence is read into a protein, and how cells decide which genes to read.

modules.title: Mutation and single-gene inheritance
modules.summary: What different changes do to a protein, and how to read offspring counts to infer genotypes and gene interactions.

modules.title: Inheritance in families
modules.summary: Linked genes, pedigrees and carrier chances, and traits that have many causes.

lessons.title: Genes, variants and the rest of the genome
lessons.objective: Place a DNA difference on the genome's map (protein-coding exon, regulatory sequence, RNA gene or the DNA between genes), judge how likely it is to matter, and use the words gene, allele and variant correctly.

concepts.title: Gene
concepts.summary: A stretch of DNA that is a unit of heredity; about 19,900 human genes code for proteins and many others make RNA or help control other genes.

concepts.title: Allele and variant
concepts.summary: Alleles are forms of the same gene that differ in sequence; a variant is any permanent change in the DNA sequence, and most variants have no effect on health.

concepts.title: Noncoding DNA
concepts.summary: About 99 percent of human DNA does not code for protein, and some of it holds regulatory elements, RNA genes and chromosome structures.

concepts.title: SNP
concepts.summary: A single-letter difference found in at least 1 percent of people; most lie between genes and have no effect, but they can act as markers.

misconceptions: Most of the genome is genes. Only about 1 percent of DNA is protein-coding.
Noncoding DNA is junk, so a change there cannot matter. Some of it holds the elements that decide when genes are on.
A person 'has the cystic fibrosis gene'. Everyone has CFTR; disease follows from variants that stop it working.
Any DNA difference changes a protein. Most SNPs lie between genes and have no effect.
Two people differ at many genes. They differ at millions of positions, yet more than 99 percent of bases are the same.
sequence: Start from the scale: about 3 billion bases, about 19,900 protein-coding genes, 1 percent of the DNA coding. Ask what the other 99 percent is for.
Name what lives in noncoding DNA: regulatory elements, RNA genes, introns, telomeres and centromeres, the stretches between genes.
Define allele and variant by comparing two people at one position; place SNPs (about one per 1,000 nucleotides, 4 to 5 million per person).
Show where SNPs usually fall (between genes) and why most do nothing, while a few in a coding or regulatory spot do.
Correct the phrase 'the gene for X': genes do not cause disease, variants that alter or remove their function do.
Recap as a habit: for any DNA difference ask where it falls, then what that location can do.
examples: A substitution that changes Glu to Val inside the HBB coding region, versus a substitution in the DNA between two genes: the first can change a protein, the second most likely changes nothing.
5 million SNPs against 3 billion bases is about 0.17 percent (derived), consistent with 'more than 99 percent the same'.
'The cystic fibrosis gene' on chromosome 7 is CFTR, which every person carries; some versions of it carry a disease-causing variant.

figures.shows: A chromosome strip with exons (solid blocks), introns, a promoter and enhancer, an RNA gene and long stretches between genes, with six SNP markers labelled A to F and no verdicts.
figures.learnerAction: Tap a marker to read where it falls (not what it does) and drag it into a category.

figures.shows: Four numbers side by side: bases in a genome, protein-coding genes, share of DNA that codes, SNPs per genome.
figures.learnerAction: none

questionPlan.sample: Sort six single-base changes by what each location can do: (1) changes an amino acid inside a coding exon; (2) falls in an enhancer for a gene; (3) falls in the DNA between two genes with no known role; (4) falls in a gene for a transfer RNA; (5) falls in a second stretch between genes; (6) falls in a coding exon at a third codon position where the amino acid stays the same. Categories: can change the protein's amino acids / can change how much or when protein is made / can change a non-protein RNA / most likely no effect.
questionPlan.answer: 1 amino acids; 2 how much or when; 3 most likely no effect; 4 non-protein RNA; 5 most likely no effect; 6 most likely no effect
questionPlan.why: Location decides what a change can do. A third-position change that keeps the amino acid (the code is degenerate) and a change between genes are both most likely harmless; a regulatory change alters amount, not sequence.

questionPlan.sample: A news story says a patient 'has the cystic fibrosis gene'. Which reading is accurate?
questionPlan.answer: Everyone has the CFTR gene; the patient has a version with a variant that disrupts it
choices: Only people with cystic fibrosis have the gene
Everyone has the CFTR gene; the patient has a version with a variant that disrupts it
The patient gained an extra gene that others lack
Carriers of one variant have no working CFTR gene
questionPlan.why: The first wrong option treats the gene as the disease; genes do not cause disease, variants that change their function do. The second treats a variant as a new gene. The third says carriers lack the gene, which nobody does.

questionPlan.sample: Two unrelated people have their genomes compared. Each differs from a reference at about 4 to 5 million SNPs. Which statement fits the numbers?
questionPlan.answer: They differ at millions of positions yet are still more than 99 percent identical
choices: They differ at about 1 percent of positions
They differ at millions of positions yet are still more than 99 percent identical
They differ only in a few hundred genes and are otherwise identical
They differ at no more than a few thousand positions
questionPlan.why: 5 million of 3 billion is about 0.17 percent. 'About 1 percent different' overstates by six times. 'Differ in only a few genes' mistakes where the differences are: most lie between genes. 'Identical' ignores the millions of sites.

questionPlan.sample: A study finds that a SNP in the DNA between two genes is more common in people with a disease. What is the most reasonable first reading?
questionPlan.answer: It marks a region worth examining; it may regulate a nearby gene or simply travel with one that does
choices: The SNP must be changing a protein's amino acids
It marks a region worth examining; it may regulate a nearby gene or simply travel with one that does
DNA between genes is junk, so the association is a mistake
The disease gene is the SNP itself
questionPlan.why: 'Must change a protein' ignores that it lies between genes. 'Junk, so ignore' ignores that noncoding DNA holds regulatory elements and that SNPs act as markers. Neither extreme is supported.

questionPlan.sample: Two people each carry two copies of HBB. They differ at one base in one copy. What do we call the two versions of HBB?
questionPlan.answer: alleles (accept: variants)
questionPlan.why: Alleles are forms of the same gene that differ in sequence.

lessons.title: Reading the genetic code
lessons.objective: Translate a coding sequence into amino acids with the standard codon table, find where translation starts and stops, and say which changes to a codon alter the protein.

concepts.title: Gene expression
concepts.summary: Transcription copies a gene's information into messenger RNA; translation reads that mRNA to build a protein.

concepts.title: Codon and reading frame
concepts.summary: A codon is three nucleotides; reading proceeds in non-overlapping triplets from the start, so the frame fixes every amino acid.

concepts.title: Start and stop codons
concepts.summary: AUG starts translation and reads as methionine; three codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) code for no amino acid and end the chain.

concepts.title: Degeneracy
concepts.summary: Several codons can name the same amino acid, but no codon names two; changes at the third position are often silent.

misconceptions: The three-letter codons overlap, so each base is read three times. They are read in non-overlapping triplets.
One codon, one amino acid. Many amino acids have several codons; each codon names only one.
Every codon is an amino acid. Three codons are stop signals.
The ribosome can start anywhere. It starts at an AUG, and the first codon fixes the frame.
Proteins are built straight from the DNA. mRNA carries the message out of the nucleus first.
sequence: Open with expression: two steps, transcription then translation, and the ribosome reading codons.
Read the NCBI table as four aligned rows: the first, second and third base of each codon sit in the same column as its amino acid, with three stops marked.
Translate a short mRNA by hand, codon by codon, stopping at a stop codon.
Slide the reading frame by one base and watch the protein change completely.
Introduce degeneracy with GAA and GAG, then ask which single-base changes keep the amino acid.
Recap the three habits: find the start, keep the frame, stop at a stop.
examples: AUG AAA UGG CAU UAA GGG reads Met-Lys-Trp-His then stops at UAA; GGG is never translated (checked against the table in the pack).
The same string read one base later, UGA AAU GGC AUU AAG, begins with a stop codon and gives no protein.
GAA names Glu. GAG also names Glu (silent); GAU names Asp; CAA names Gln; UAA is a stop.

figures.shows: The standard code as the pack gives it: Base1, Base2, Base3 rows over an AAs row, laid out as a 4 by 4 by 4 grid.
figures.learnerAction: Pick three bases and read the amino acid; no answers are shown for the practice strings.

figures.shows: An mRNA strip with a bracket showing the reading frame and a ribosome marker that can be set to frame 1, 2 or 3.
figures.learnerAction: Slide the frame and read the amino acids that appear.

questionPlan.sample: How many amino acids does 5'-AUGAAAUGGCAUUAAGGG-3' encode, reading from the first base?
questionPlan.why: AUG, AAA, UGG, CAU give Met, Lys, Trp, His; UAA is a stop, so GGG is never translated.

questionPlan.sample: The same mRNA, AUGAAAUGGCAUUAAGGG, is read starting at the second base. What happens?
questionPlan.answer: Translation ends at once because the first codon, UGA, is a stop
choices: The same four amino acids appear one position later
Translation ends at once because the first codon, UGA, is a stop
The protein is Lys-Trp-His
Only the first amino acid changes
questionPlan.why: A one-base shift changes every codon. 'Same protein shifted along' treats the code as a sliding message; 'Lys-Trp-His' keeps the old codons although the triplets have changed.

questionPlan.sample: Codon GAA names glutamic acid. Which single-base change leaves the amino acid unchanged?
questionPlan.answer: GAA to GAG
choices: GAA to GAU
GAA to CAA
GAA to GAG
GAA to UAA
questionPlan.why: GAU names Asp and CAA names Gln (missense); UAA is a stop (nonsense). Only the third-position change to GAG still names Glu, which is what degeneracy permits.

questionPlan.sample: Put these in order: the ribosome stops at a stop codon and releases the chain; the gene's information is copied to mRNA; the ribosome starts at AUG; mRNA moves into the cytoplasm; tRNA adds amino acids one at a time.
answer: The gene's information is copied to mRNA
tRNA adds amino acids one at a time
The ribosome stops at a stop codon and releases the chain
questionPlan.why: Transcription comes before translation, translation starts at AUG and ends at a stop codon.

questionPlan.sample: In 5'-AUGAAAUGGCAUUAAGGG-3', what becomes of GGG, which follows the UAA?
questionPlan.answer: It is not translated because the ribosome has already stopped
choices: It adds a glycine to the end
It is not translated because the ribosome has already stopped
It is read as the start of a second protein
It is removed from the DNA
questionPlan.why: UAA is a stop codon, which codes for no amino acid and ends the chain. Treating it as 'a codon for Gly later' mistakes the stop for a pause.

lessons.title: Switching genes on and off
lessons.objective: Predict whether a gene is expressed from the cell's conditions and the state of its regulatory sequences and proteins, using the lac operon as a worked system, and explain how one genome gives different cell types.

concepts.title: Gene regulation
concepts.summary: Each cell expresses only some of its genes at a time; control is mostly at transcription, where regulatory proteins raise or lower it.

concepts.title: Repressor and operator
concepts.summary: In the lac operon a repressor protein bound to the operator blocks RNA polymerase; lactose binding releases it.

concepts.title: Cis and trans
concepts.summary: A regulatory DNA sequence acts only on genes on the same DNA (cis); a diffusible protein can act on both copies in a cell (trans).

concepts.title: Enhancers and transcription factors
concepts.summary: In eukaryotes, enhancers bind tissue-specific factors, so different cell types switch on different genes from the same DNA.

misconceptions: Cells with different jobs have different DNA. Nearly every cell has the same DNA; they express different genes.
A gene is either on or off. Control is graded: lactose alone gives moderate expression, lactose without glucose gives high.
A normal copy of a gene elsewhere in the cell rescues a broken operator. An operator acts only on the DNA it sits on (cis).
A repressor is always bound. It binds the operator unless lactose has changed its shape.
Regulation happens only by switching transcription off. Activators such as CAP raise it.
sequence: Begin with the puzzle: a liver cell and a muscle cell carry the same DNA and make different proteins.
Lay out the lac operon: promoter, operator, three enzyme genes on one transcript, and the repressor made elsewhere.
Walk the four conditions (lactose present or absent, glucose present or absent) and the repressor and CAP states in each.
Introduce constitutive mutants (no repressor, broken operator) and the never-inducible super-repressor.
Use partial diploids to separate cis from trans.
Move to eukaryotes: enhancers, transcription factors, and the modular yellow gene.
examples: No lactose: operator occupied, off. Lactose present, glucose present: repressor released, moderate. Lactose present, glucose absent: CAP with cAMP raises it, high.

Chromosome I+ Oc Z- with an F factor I+ O+ Z+ (derived from the cis rule): no functional beta-galactosidase without lactose, because the operon carrying Oc has the broken Z gene and the intact operon is still repressed.
The yellow gene has separate enhancers for wing, body and mouth; deleting only the wing enhancer should remove pigment in the wing only (inference from the pack's modular description).

figures.shows: The lac operon as a strip (promoter, operator, lacZ, lacY, lacA) with the repressor and CAP drawn as separate proteins; switchable views for each of four conditions.
figures.learnerAction: Set lactose and glucose to present or absent and see which proteins are bound; output level hidden until the learner commits to a prediction.

figures.shows: Two copies of the operon in one cell (chromosome and F factor) with a mutation selector for each copy.
figures.learnerAction: Choose the mutation on each copy and predict enzyme made with and without lactose.

questionPlan.sample: E. coli grows with lactose and no glucose. What is the state of the lac operon?
questionPlan.answer: High transcription: lactose has released the repressor and CAP bound to cAMP boosts transcription
choices: Off, because the repressor is bound to the operator
Moderate transcription: the repressor is released but nothing boosts it
High transcription: lactose has released the repressor and CAP bound to cAMP boosts transcription
High transcription whatever the glucose level
questionPlan.why: 'Off' forgets that lactose releases the repressor. 'Moderate only' forgets that low glucose raises cAMP and so CAP activation. 'High whatever the glucose' ignores the pack's rule that high expression needs glucose absent.

questionPlan.sample: Which mutant could not be switched on even with lactose present?
questionPlan.answer: One whose repressor cannot bind lactose
choices: One with no working repressor protein
One with an operator the repressor cannot bind
One whose repressor cannot bind lactose
One with extra copies of lacZ
questionPlan.why: A repressor that cannot bind lactose stays on the operator (the super-repressor). A mutant with no working repressor or a broken operator is always on instead.

questionPlan.sample: A cell has two copies of the operon. Copy 1 has a broken operator (Oc) and a dead lacZ. Copy 2 is normal. The cell makes a working repressor. With no lactose, does it make working beta-galactosidase?
questionPlan.answer: No: the broken operator acts only on its own DNA, whose lacZ is dead, and the normal copy is still repressed
choices: Yes, because the normal lacZ is present in the cell
Yes, because the broken operator switches on both copies
No: the broken operator acts only on its own DNA, whose lacZ is dead, and the normal copy is still repressed
No, because the cell lacks lactose and so lacks every enzyme
questionPlan.why: 'Yes, the normal lacZ makes enzyme' forgets that the normal copy's operator is bound by repressor. 'Yes, Oc switches on both copies' forgets that an operator mutation acts only in cis.

questionPlan.sample: A liver cell and a muscle cell from one person make different proteins. What explains it?
questionPlan.answer: They carry the same DNA but express different genes through different transcription factors and enhancers
choices: Each cell type keeps only the genes it needs
They carry the same DNA but express different genes through different transcription factors and enhancers
Mutations in each tissue change its genes
Muscle cells carry different chromosomes
questionPlan.why: 'Different DNA' is wrong: nearly every cell has the same DNA. 'Random mutation' would not give reproducible cell types. 'Different chromosomes' repeats the DNA error.

questionPlan.sample: The yellow gene has separate enhancers for wing, body and mouth. A fly lacks only the wing enhancer. What would you predict?
questionPlan.answer: Yellow pigment is missing in the wing but present in body and mouth
choices: Pigment is missing everywhere
Pigment is missing in the wing but present in body and mouth
Pigment is normal because the promoter remains
Pigment is made in the wing at double the rate
questionPlan.why: Each enhancer drives expression in one tissue, so removing one removes expression there only. 'Missing everywhere' treats the gene as one switch; 'normal' ignores the wing enhancer's role.

lessons.title: What a mutation does to a protein
lessons.objective: Classify a DNA change as silent, missense, nonsense, in-frame deletion or frameshift from the codon table, and predict from the kind of change and the gene's dosage needs whether an allele will behave as recessive or dominant.

concepts.title: Silent, missense and nonsense
concepts.summary: A substitution may keep the amino acid (silent), swap it (missense) or create a stop (nonsense).

concepts.title: Insertions, deletions and the frame
concepts.summary: An insertion or deletion that is not a multiple of three shifts every codon downstream (frameshift); a multiple of three adds or removes whole amino acids.

concepts.title: Loss and gain of function
concepts.summary: Alleles lose function completely (amorph) or partly (hypomorph), gain more of it (hypermorph), gain a new one (neomorph) or poison the normal product (antimorph).

concepts.title: Haplosufficient and haploinsufficient
concepts.summary: If one good copy makes enough product the null allele is recessive; if not, it is dominant.

misconceptions: Every mutation is harmful. Most variants have no effect on health.
Any deletion causes a frameshift. A deletion of three bases keeps the frame and removes one amino acid.
An in-frame deletion is harmless. The common cystic fibrosis allele removes one amino acid and the protein misfolds.
A loss-of-function allele is always recessive. If one copy does not make enough product, it is dominant.
Missense and nonsense are the same. One swaps an amino acid; the other ends the chain early.
sequence: Open with sickle cell: one amino-acid change (Glu to Val at position 6 of beta-globin) from a single-base change.
Classify substitutions with the table: silent, missense, nonsense.
Show insertions and deletions, and why only multiples of three keep the frame.
Grade function: null, partial, more, new, interfering.
Link function to dominance through dosage: one good copy suffices for most genes, not all.
Close on cystic fibrosis: more than a thousand alleles, one common three-base deletion that misfolds the protein.
examples: Reading ATG GAG GTG CAC as Met-Glu-Val-His: GAG to GAA is silent; GAG to GTG is missense (Glu to Val); GAG to TAG is nonsense; deleting the fourth base gives Met-Arg-Cys; deleting GAG gives Met-Val-His; inserting CC after ATG gives Met-Pro-Arg-Cys (all checked against the pack's table).
Hemoglobin S: the pack states Glu6Val. In the table Glu is GAA or GAG and Val is GTN, so one A-to-T change in the middle base gets from one to the other (derived).
If a dimer protein carries a mutant subunit that poisons it and subunits pair at random, only 1 in 4 dimers is normal in a heterozygote (assumption stated); a null heterozygote keeps 1 in 2.

figures.shows: Three aligned rows (DNA, mRNA, protein) for a four-codon gene, with a base editor the learner can change.
figures.learnerAction: Change one base or delete bases and read the new protein; the category label stays hidden until the learner names it.

figures.shows: Five allele classes with columns for what the product does and how a heterozygote behaves (left blank for dominance).
figures.learnerAction: Fill the dominance column.

questionPlan.sample: Gene reads ATG GAG GTG CAC (Met-Glu-Val-His). Sort the six changes: (a) GAG to GAA; (b) GAG to GTG; (c) GAG to TAG; (d) delete the fourth base; (e) delete GAG; (f) insert two bases after ATG. Categories: silent / missense / nonsense / frameshift / in-frame deletion.
questionPlan.answer: a silent; b missense; c nonsense; d frameshift; e in-frame deletion; f frameshift
questionPlan.why: The table decides a, b and c; the count of bases decides d to f: one or two bases shift the frame, three do not.

questionPlan.sample: The common cystic fibrosis allele deletes three nucleotides, keeping the reading frame, and removes one phenylalanine from a protein of 1,480 amino acids. Why is it still severe?
questionPlan.answer: The missing amino acid makes the protein fold wrongly, so it never reaches the cell membrane
choices: The deletion shifts the reading frame
The deletion creates a premature stop codon
The missing amino acid makes the protein fold wrongly, so it never reaches the cell membrane
The deleted bases lie in noncoding DNA
questionPlan.why: A frameshift would need a non-multiple of three. A new stop codon is not described. 'Deletions in noncoding DNA' contradicts that the phenylalanine is lost from the protein.

questionPlan.sample: A null allele of an enzyme gene is recessive: heterozygotes are healthy. Why?
questionPlan.answer: One working copy makes enough enzyme for a normal phenotype
choices: Null alleles are recessive in every gene
One working copy makes enough enzyme for a normal phenotype
The good copy repairs the mutant protein
The mutant allele is silenced in heterozygotes
questionPlan.why: Most genes are haplosufficient. 'Null alleles are always recessive' is the trap: some genes need both copies. 'The mutant allele is switched off' and 'the good copy repairs the bad' invent mechanisms.

questionPlan.sample: For another gene, a single working copy is not enough and heterozygous carriers of a null allele are affected. What is that property of the gene called?
questionPlan.answer: haploinsufficient
questionPlan.why: One wild-type copy does not supply enough product, so the loss-of-function allele shows as dominant.

questionPlan.sample: A protein works only as a dimer. A mutant subunit joins normal subunits and disables the dimer. In a heterozygote, with half the subunits mutant and subunits pairing at random, what percentage of dimers are fully normal?
questionPlan.why: Both subunits must be normal: 1/2 times 1/2 = 1/4. A null heterozygote would keep 50 percent of its dimers, so this allele is worse than a null (antimorph).

lessons.title: Reading offspring ratios
lessons.objective: Infer parent genotypes and the relationship between genes from offspring counts: test cross, incomplete dominance and codominance, 9:3:3:1 and its modified forms, and sex linkage from reciprocal crosses.

concepts.title: Test cross
concepts.summary: Crossing an individual of unknown genotype to a homozygous recessive reveals its genotype from the offspring ratio.

concepts.title: Incomplete dominance and codominance
concepts.summary: In incomplete dominance the heterozygote is intermediate; in codominance it shows both alleles at once.

concepts.title: Dihybrid ratios and epistasis
concepts.summary: Independent loci give 9:3:3:1; when one locus masks another the classes merge (9:3:4, 12:3:1).

concepts.title: Sex linkage and reciprocal crosses
concepts.summary: Reciprocal crosses that differ, with sons and daughters unlike, point to an X-linked gene in a hemizygous male.

misconceptions: Observed ratios should match the expected ones exactly. Real counts scatter; a test decides whether the gap is chance.
Incomplete dominance blends alleles for good. The alleles stay separate and segregate again.
Codominance gives an intermediate. The heterozygote shows both phenotypes, not a blend.
A 9:3:4 ratio means linked genes. It is two genes interacting (epistasis); linkage shows in a different way.
X-linked traits cannot appear in females. A female with two recessive alleles is affected.
sequence: Open with a purple-flowered plant whose genotype is unknown and show that a test cross answers it.
Add allele relationships: incomplete dominance (pink carnations) and codominance (ABO).
Predict 9:3:3:1 with the product rule, then show how masking merges classes.
Introduce sex linkage and the reciprocal-cross test.
Close on noise: counts are never exact; chi-square is the tool geneticists use to judge a gap.
Recap as a decision list: count the classes, name the ratio, name the mechanism.
examples: A purple plant crossed to white gives 49 purple and 51 white (about 1:1), so the purple parent was Aa; all offspring purple would point to AA.
Labrador cross, 160 pups: expected 90 black, 30 chocolate, 40 yellow (9:3:4); an invented count of 88, 33, 39 fits and has three classes, not four.
Red female by white male gives all-red offspring; white female by red male gives red daughters and white sons: reciprocal crosses differ, so the gene is X-linked.

figures.shows: A bag of gametes drawn at random 20, 100 and 1,000 times for an Aa x aa test cross, showing how the ratio settles.
figures.learnerAction: Draw samples and watch the gap from 1:1 narrow.

figures.shows: Bars for phenotype classes beside the expected 9:3:3:1, 9:3:4 and 12:3:1 shapes.
figures.learnerAction: Match a count to a ratio; hidden answers until commit.

questionPlan.sample: A purple-flowered plant is crossed to a white-flowered plant (aa). The 100 offspring are 49 purple and 51 white. What was the purple parent's genotype?
questionPlan.answer: Aa
choices: AA
Aa
aa
Cannot be told without a second cross
questionPlan.why: A 1:1 ratio means the purple parent made two kinds of gamete, so it was heterozygous. AA would give all purple offspring; 3:1 appears in a cross of two heterozygotes, not a test cross.

questionPlan.sample: Two Labrador retrievers heterozygous at both coat-colour loci (B and E) produce 160 pups: 88 black, 33 chocolate, 39 yellow. Which ratio and explanation fit best?
questionPlan.answer: 9:3:4, because one locus (E) masks the other when ee
choices: 9:3:3:1, with two independent loci
9:3:4, because one locus (E) masks the other when ee
12:3:1, because a dominant allele masks the other locus
3:1, with one locus
questionPlan.why: Three classes rule out 9:3:3:1 (four classes) and 3:1. 12:3:1 would need a dominant masking allele. The data show 9:3:4 from recessive epistasis.

questionPlan.sample: Red-eyed female by white-eyed male gives all red-eyed offspring. White-eyed female by red-eyed male gives red-eyed daughters and white-eyed sons. What explains it?
questionPlan.answer: The gene is on the X chromosome and white is recessive
choices: The gene is autosomal and white is recessive
The gene is on the X chromosome and white is recessive
The gene is on the Y chromosome
The gene is autosomal and white is dominant
questionPlan.why: An autosomal gene gives the same result from reciprocal crosses; here results differ and sons differ from daughters. 'Dominant white' predicts white-eyed offspring from the first cross.

questionPlan.sample: One parent has blood type AB and the other type O (ii). Which blood types can their children have?
questionPlan.answer: A or B only
choices: A, B, AB or O
A or B only
AB only
O only
questionPlan.why: The AB parent gives IA or IB, the O parent gives i, so children are IAi (A) or IBi (B). AB needs two non-i alleles; O needs an i from each parent.

questionPlan.sample: Two pink carnations (one red allele, one white allele; incomplete dominance) are crossed and give 400 offspring. About how many are pink?
questionPlan.why: Genotypes AA:Aa:aa come out 1:2:1 and the heterozygote is pink: one half of 400.

questionPlan.sample: A cross is expected to give 1:1 and gives 62:38. Which tool tells you whether chance alone could produce a gap that size?
questionPlan.answer: A chi-square goodness-of-fit test
choices: Any gap shows the genotype assumption is wrong
A chi-square goodness-of-fit test
Repeat the cross until the ratio is exactly 1:1
Count only the larger class
questionPlan.why: Any gap does not prove the model wrong, and ratios are never exact; a statistical test decides. Doubling the sample would not itself settle it.

lessons.title: Linked genes and recombination
lessons.objective: Compute a recombination frequency from test-cross counts, decide whether two genes are linked, and convert it to a map distance, taking account of which arrangement the parents carried.

concepts.title: Linkage
concepts.summary: Loci close together on one chromosome tend to be inherited together, an exception to independent assortment.

concepts.title: Recombination frequency
concepts.summary: The share of gametes (or test-cross offspring) that carry a combination not found in the parents' chromosomes; about 50 percent for unlinked loci and the most that can be observed.

concepts.title: Coupling and repulsion
concepts.summary: A dihybrid AaBb may carry AB and ab together (coupling) or Ab and aB (repulsion); the parents' genotypes decide which offspring are recombinant.

concepts.title: Map units
concepts.summary: A recombination frequency of 1 percent is about 1 centiMorgan, accurate for short distances; double crossovers hide recombination at long ones.

misconceptions: Linked genes never recombine. Crossovers separate them in some meioses.
The most common classes are always the dominant-dominant ones. The parental classes are fixed by the chromosomes the parents supplied.
A recombination frequency can reach 80 percent. About 50 percent is the maximum, reached by unlinked or very distant loci.
A genotype AaBb shows how the alleles sit. It does not say which are on the same chromosome.
Map distance in cM is exact and additive for any distance. Double crossovers make long distances underestimates.
sequence: Start from Mendel's independent assortment and ask when it fails.
Define recombinant and parental gametes by what the parents supplied, including coupling and repulsion.
Run a test cross on a dihybrid and read four classes.
Compute the recombination frequency and call the loci linked or unlinked.
Convert to centiMorgans and say where the approximation fails (double crossovers).
Recap as: say the arrangement first, then count.
examples: Pack data: 48 short-brown, 42 long-white, 13 short-white, 17 long-brown offspring from a test cross; recombinants 13 + 17 = 30 of 120, so RF = 25 percent.
Invented test-cross counts 38, 44, 9, 9: recombinants 18 of 100, RF = 18 percent, about 18 cM.

Same four counts 412, 388, 98, 102 read two ways: with parents AB/ab the recombinants are 98 + 102 = 200 of 1,000 (20 percent); read as repulsion, recombinants would be 80 percent, above the 50 percent maximum, so that reading is wrong.

figures.shows: A pair of homologous chromosomes with alleles on them and a crossover that can be switched on or off between the two loci; the four resulting gametes are listed.
figures.learnerAction: Switch the crossover and say which gametes are parental and which recombinant.

figures.shows: A four-row count table from a test cross with columns for phenotype, number, gamete and parental or recombinant (last column blank).
figures.learnerAction: Fill the last column and compute RF.

questionPlan.sample: A dihybrid with alleles in coupling is test-crossed. The 100 offspring include 38 and 44 with parental combinations and 9 and 9 with recombinant combinations. What is the recombination frequency in percent?
questionPlan.why: Recombinants 9 + 9 = 18 of 100, so RF = 18 percent, about 18 cM.

questionPlan.sample: A test cross gives AaBb 412, aabb 388, Aabb 98, aaBb 102. If the parent's chromosomes carried A with b and a with B, what would the recombination frequency come to?
questionPlan.answer: 80 percent, which is impossible, so the parent must have carried AB and ab
choices: 20 percent
80 percent, which is impossible, so the parent must have carried AB and ab
50 percent, so the genes are unlinked
Cannot be calculated
questionPlan.why: Reading the Aabb and aaBb classes as parental gives 800 recombinants of 1,000, over the 50 percent ceiling, so the arrangement was assumed wrongly. The mistake of calling the largest classes 'parental' without checking the parents is the trap.

questionPlan.sample: Two loci give a recombination frequency of about 50 percent. What does that tell you?
questionPlan.answer: They are on different chromosomes or far apart on the same one
choices: They are tightly linked
They are on different chromosomes or far apart on the same one
They have been mapped wrongly
They are in repulsion
questionPlan.why: Fifty percent is the ceiling, not a linkage figure: multiple crossovers between distant loci act like independent assortment. 'Tightly linked' reads the number backwards.

questionPlan.sample: Loci A and B are 12 cM apart, B and C are 8 cM apart, and A and C are 4 cM apart. Put them in order along the chromosome.
questionPlan.why: A-to-B (12) = A-to-C (4) + C-to-B (8), so C lies between A and B (derived from combining pairwise distances).

questionPlan.sample: Two loci at opposite ends of a chromosome more than 100 cM long are crossed. Why is their recombination frequency not above 100 percent?
questionPlan.answer: Multiple crossovers between them return parental combinations, so the frequency tops out near 50 percent
choices: Chromosomes longer than 100 cM do not exist
Multiple crossovers between them return parental combinations, so the frequency tops out near 50 percent
Crossovers stop beyond 50 cM
The test cross fails for long chromosomes
questionPlan.why: Map units add up beyond 100 but observed recombination does not: a double crossover looks parental. 'Chromosomes cannot be that long' contradicts the pack.

lessons.title: Reading a pedigree
lessons.objective: Decide which modes of inheritance a pedigree allows, rule modes out from specific features, and work out a carrier probability by chaining the Mendelian chances through the family.

concepts.title: Pedigree
concepts.summary: A family tree of one trait, with circles for females, squares for males, filled symbols for affected people and a proband who brought the family to attention.

concepts.title: Features of each mode
concepts.summary: Autosomal dominant: every affected person has an affected parent. Autosomal recessive: unaffected parents can have affected children. X-linked recessive: mostly males, never an affected daughter of an unaffected father.

concepts.title: Carrier probability
concepts.summary: An unaffected child of two carriers is a carrier with probability 2/3; chances along a chain multiply (and alternatives add).

concepts.title: Each pregnancy independent
concepts.summary: Chances for a recessive condition are 1/4 per pregnancy whatever happened before.

misconceptions: Dominant traits never skip a generation. In a small family an affected heterozygous parent can pass the normal allele to every child, so a dominant trait can appear to skip.
An unaffected sibling of an affected child is a carrier with chance 1/2. It is 2/3 once the affected genotype is excluded.
X-linked recessive traits never affect females. A female is affected if her father is affected and her mother carries the allele.
After an affected child the next is safe, or is certain to be affected. Each pregnancy has the same chance (1 in 4).
A disease that runs in a family is genetic. Shared environment or sporadic cases can explain it.
sequence: Define the symbols and the proband, then state the six modes by their features.

Rule modes out: unaffected parents with an affected child exclude dominant modes; an affected daughter of an unaffected father excludes X-linked recessive; an affected father with an unaffected mother outside the family cannot pass an X-linked trait to a son.
Pick the most likely remaining mode.
Compute chances: 1/4 for two carriers, 2/3 for an unaffected child of two carriers.
Chain them with a partner's population carrier chance.
Close with the cautions: some conditions run in families without being inherited, and most pedigrees contain errors.
examples: Pedigree A (autosomal recessive): parents I-1 and I-2 unaffected; children II-1 affected daughter, II-2 unaffected son, II-3 unaffected daughter. II-3 is a carrier with chance 2/3; with an unrelated partner whose carrier chance is 1/25 (cystic fibrosis in people of European descent, from the pack) a child is affected with chance 2/3 x 1/25 x 1/4 = 1/150 (derived).

Pedigree B (X-linked recessive): affected father I-1, unaffected mother I-2; daughters II-1, II-2 unaffected; a grandson III-1 affected. Each daughter is a carrier for certain; each of her sons is affected with chance 1/2.
Pedigree C (autosomal dominant): affected in every generation, an affected father with an affected son, so X-linked dominant is out.

figures.shows: Three drawn pedigrees A, B and C (as described under Examples), with a mode-of-inheritance checklist beside each that the learner ticks or crosses.
figures.learnerAction: Tap each mode to rule it in or out; tap an unaffected person to enter a carrier probability.

figures.shows: Rows for the six modes and columns for the one feature that best identifies each, filled in only after the learner ticks the modes on a pedigree.
figures.learnerAction: none

questionPlan.sample: Pedigree A: two unaffected parents have an affected daughter. Which mode fits?
questionPlan.answer: Autosomal recessive
choices: Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
X-linked dominant
questionPlan.why: Dominant modes need an affected parent. X-linked recessive needs an affected father for an affected daughter. Only autosomal recessive allows unaffected parents with an affected daughter.

questionPlan.sample: In Pedigree A, II-3 is unaffected, with two unaffected carrier parents. What is the probability that II-3 is a carrier, as a fraction or decimal?
questionPlan.answer: 2/3 (accept 0.67)
questionPlan.why: Of the 1:2:1 genotypes only AA and Aa remain once aa is excluded, so Aa is 2 of 3.

questionPlan.sample: II-3 and an unrelated partner (carrier chance 1 in 25) have a child. What is the chance it is affected, as 1 in how many?
A couple have one child with an autosomal recessive condition. What is the chance the next child is affected?
questionPlan.answer: 1 in 4 (25 percent)
choices: Nil: they have had their affected child
1 in 4 (25 percent)
1 in 16
1 in 2
questionPlan.why: Each pregnancy is independent. 'Safe' and 'certain' both treat the first child as changing the chance; 1 in 16 multiplies two births.

questionPlan.sample: Four members of a family in one house have the same illness, and a water test shows contamination. What should a counsellor conclude before drawing a pedigree?
questionPlan.answer: A shared environment could explain it, so a genetic cause is not established
choices: It is autosomal dominant
It is autosomal recessive
A shared environment could explain it, so a genetic cause is not established
It is mitochondrial
questionPlan.why: Conditions can run in families because family members share exposures. A mode of inheritance only makes sense once a genetic cause is plausible.

lessons.title: Traits with many causes
lessons.objective: Say what penetrance, expressivity and heritability each mean, and decide from a case whether a pattern points to one gene with incomplete penetrance, to many genes plus environment, or to a shared environment.

concepts.title: Penetrance
concepts.summary: The share of people with a particular variant who show the associated trait or disorder.

concepts.title: Expressivity
concepts.summary: The range of severity among people with the same variant.

concepts.title: Heritability
concepts.summary: A statistic for how much of the variation in a trait, in one population and environment, goes with genetic differences; it is not the share of a trait caused by genes.

concepts.title: Polygenic and multifactorial
concepts.summary: Many variants of small effect plus environment, with no clear-cut inheritance pattern.

misconceptions: A heritability of 0.7 means 70 percent of a trait is caused by genes. It means 70 percent of the variation in that population goes with genetic differences.
Heritable means familial. Language is familial and not heritable.
High heritability means the trait cannot be changed. Hair colour is highly heritable and easy to dye.
Carrying a risk variant means getting the disorder. Penetrance is often below 100 percent (BRCA).
Heritability points to specific genes. It tells nothing about which genes or environments are involved.
sequence: Start from Genotype plus Environment, and a disorder where not everyone with the variant is affected.
Define penetrance and expressivity with BRCA and FBN1 as the two examples.
Move to many genes: height as polygenic, with FGFR3 achondroplasia as the single-gene extreme.
Define heritability from twins and state its four limits.
Show that environment can move a highly heritable trait: height in immigrant families.
Recap as three questions to ask of any trait claim: which people, which environment, which kind of effect.
examples: A BRCA1 or BRCA2 variant carrier may never develop cancer (reduced penetrance); two people with an FBN1 variant can have mild or life-threatening Marfan features (variable expressivity).
About 80 percent of height is stated to go with inherited variants and more than 700 variants are known; the same page says prediction for one child is hard.
Heritability of 0.7 for a trait means 70 percent of the variation among people in that population goes with genetic differences, not that a person's height is 70 percent genetic.

figures.shows: Dot strips for two populations: the same trait, the same genetic differences, but different average values (environment shift), plus a dot for one person.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the environment slider and watch the spread keep its shape while the average moves.

figures.shows: Four statements about a trait in two columns: 'what heritability says' and 'what it does not say', unfilled.
figures.learnerAction: Sort statements into the two columns.

questionPlan.sample: Sort these cases under penetrance, expressivity, heritability or familial but not heritable: (1) A woman with a BRCA1 variant reaches 80 without cancer; (2) siblings with the same FBN1 variant, one mild, one with heart complications; (3) in one population 80 percent of variation in height goes with genetic differences; (4) relatives all speak the same language.
questionPlan.answer: 1 penetrance; 2 expressivity; 3 heritability; 4 familial but not heritable
questionPlan.why: Penetrance is whether the trait appears, expressivity how strongly, heritability a population statistic, and sharing a language is environment.

questionPlan.sample: A study reports heritability of 0.7 for a trait. Which statement is correct?
questionPlan.answer: 70 percent of the variation in the trait in that population goes with genetic differences
choices: 70 percent of each person's trait is caused by their genes
70 percent of the variation in the trait in that population goes with genetic differences
The trait cannot be changed by environment
Seven genes explain the trait
questionPlan.why: It is not the share of one person's trait that is genetic, it says nothing about which genes, and a high figure does not mean the trait is fixed.

questionPlan.sample: Average adult height rises in a population after nutrition improves, though height is highly heritable. Is that a contradiction?
questionPlan.answer: No: heritability describes variation within one population and environment, and it can change when circumstances do
choices: Yes: the heritability estimate must be wrong
No: heritability describes variation within one population and environment, and it can change when circumstances do
Yes: environment cannot affect heritable traits
No: nutrition changes the genes
questionPlan.why: The pack's immigrant-family point shows that a better environment shifted the next generation's height. Believing that high heritability means unchangeable is the trap.

questionPlan.sample: Heart disease clusters in a family but with no clear inheritance pattern. Which comparison best separates genetic from shared-household causes?
questionPlan.answer: Compare identical and fraternal twins raised together
choices: Count the number of affected relatives
Compare identical and fraternal twins raised together
Measure only the oldest generation
Test one family member for one gene
questionPlan.why: Identical twins share nearly all their DNA, fraternal twins about half; a trait more alike in identical twins points to genes. Counting affected relatives cannot separate the two.

questionPlan.sample: A person carries a high-risk BRCA2 variant and has no cancer at 60. Which statement is accurate?
questionPlan.answer: Many carriers develop cancer, but not all: the variant has reduced penetrance
choices: The test was wrong
Many carriers develop cancer, but not all: the variant has reduced penetrance
The variant is now harmless
She cannot pass the variant to her children
questionPlan.why: A carrier is at higher risk, not certain to be affected. 'The test was wrong' and 'harmless' both deny the raised risk; having no cancer says nothing about passing the variant on.

lessons.title: Hardy-Weinberg as a null model
lessons.objective: Work out allele and genotype frequencies from counts, use Hardy-Weinberg proportions to estimate how many carriers a rare recessive condition implies, and read a departure from those proportions as evidence about mating, selection or sampling.

concepts.title: Allele frequency
concepts.summary: The share of copies of a gene that are one allele; for two alleles p + q = 1, found by counting alleles (homozygotes count twice).

concepts.title: Hardy-Weinberg proportions
concepts.summary: With random mating and no other forces, genotypes occur as p squared, 2pq and q squared after one generation.

concepts.title: Carrier estimate
concepts.summary: For a rare recessive condition, carriers are about twice the square root of the birth incidence.

concepts.title: Departures
concepts.summary: Fewer heterozygotes than 2pq suggest inbreeding or population mixing; allele frequency changes over time suggest selection, drift, migration or mutation.

misconceptions: A dominant allele gains ground each generation. Without other forces frequencies stay put.
A recessive allele that is rare means few carry it. Carriers are far more common than affected (about 1 in 25 against 1 in 2,500).
q squared is the frequency of the allele. It is the frequency of the recessive homozygote.
Being in Hardy-Weinberg proportions shows there is no evolution. It shows nothing about other loci or other generations.
p squared is the frequency of the dominant phenotype. The dominant phenotype is p squared + 2pq.
sequence: Count alleles from genotypes, and see that 320, 160, 20 give p = 0.8 and q = 0.2.
Expand (p + q) squared and read off expected genotype frequencies.
List the conditions and treat the equilibrium as a null model.
Go the other way: from the incidence of a recessive disease to q, then to carriers.
Compare observed with expected counts and read the direction of the gap.
Close on the X-linked case: affected males equal q, affected females about q squared.
examples: Pack case: 320 AA, 160 Aa, 20 aa (500 people) give p = 0.8, q = 0.2 and expected 320, 160 and 20.
Cystic fibrosis incidence about 1 in 2,500: q = 0.02, carriers = 2pq about 0.039, about 1 in 25 (matches the pack's carrier figure).

Invented counts 200 AA, 80 Aa, 40 aa (320 people): p = 0.75, q = 0.25; expected 180, 120, 20; heterozygotes are 40 short and both homozygote classes are over, the signature of inbreeding or mixing of populations.

figures.shows: A square of side p + q split into four areas (p squared, two pq, q squared) with sliders for p.
figures.learnerAction: Move p and read the three genotype shares.

figures.shows: Input: incidence of a recessive disease as 1 in N. Output: q, p and carrier frequency.
figures.learnerAction: Enter an incidence and read the carrier frequency.

questionPlan.sample: A sample has 200 AA, 80 Aa and 40 aa people. What is the frequency of allele A?
questionPlan.why: A copies: 2 x 200 + 80 = 480 of 640 allele copies = 0.75.

questionPlan.sample: With those counts (p = 0.75), Hardy-Weinberg expects 180 AA, 120 Aa and 20 aa. What is the best reading of the observed 200, 80 and 40?
questionPlan.answer: There are too few heterozygotes, which suggests inbreeding or a mixed population
choices: It is in equilibrium
There are too few heterozygotes, which suggests inbreeding or a mixed population
There are too many heterozygotes, which suggests selection for them
The sample has been miscounted
questionPlan.why: Selection and drift change frequencies across generations, but a one-sample excess of homozygotes and deficit of heterozygotes is the signature of non-random mating; 'perfect equilibrium' misreads the numbers.

questionPlan.sample: A recessive condition affects 1 in 10,000 births. About what proportion of people carry one copy, as 1 in how many?
questionPlan.answer: 50 (accept 49 to 51)
questionPlan.why: q is the square root of 0.0001 = 0.01; carriers = 2pq = 2 x 0.99 x 0.01 = 0.0198, about 1 in 50 (derived).

questionPlan.sample: Red-green colour blindness affects about 1 in 12 men (q about 0.083). What does Hardy-Weinberg predict for women, as 1 in how many?
questionPlan.answer: 144 (accept 140 to 150)
questionPlan.why: Women need two copies: q squared = 1/144 = 0.007. The pack gives 0.007 expected against about 0.005 observed.

questionPlan.sample: Which statement about Hardy-Weinberg proportions is true?
questionPlan.answer: They are what you expect after random mating without selection, drift, migration or mutation, so a departure points to one of those
choices: They show that dominant alleles become common over time
They are what you expect after random mating without selection, drift, migration or mutation, so a departure points to one of those
They prove a population is not evolving
They only apply to rare alleles
questionPlan.why: The principle denies that a dominant allele spreads by being dominant and does not say natural populations meet its conditions.

lessons.title: Chance and selection in populations
lessons.objective: Decide whether chance, selection, a bottleneck or a founder event is the better explanation for a change in allele frequency or an unusually common allele, and say what evidence would separate the explanations.

concepts.title: Genetic drift
concepts.summary: Chance change in allele frequency from random sampling; it has no direction and acts faster in small populations.

concepts.title: Bottleneck and founder effect
concepts.summary: A population that shrinks, or a small group that splits off, keeps a random sample of the alleles.

concepts.title: Selection versus drift
concepts.summary: Selection pushes frequencies in a direction that depends on effects on survival and reproduction; drift can overwhelm weak selection in small populations.

concepts.title: Heterozygote advantage
concepts.summary: If carriers survive better than either homozygote, the allele is kept even though one homozygote is disabled.

misconceptions: Drift matters only in tiny populations. It acts in every population and is stronger in small ones.
Drift is guided or purposeful. It has no direction.
A common allele must be advantageous. Founder effects and drift can make harmful alleles common.
Selection removes recessive disease alleles. Carriers hide them, and carrier advantage can keep them.
A carrier advantage in mice shows it in people. The cystic fibrosis cholera idea failed in a human study.
sequence: Draw 20 marbles from a jar and see the frequencies move by chance.
Compute the four-bacteria case: equal split 6 of 16, unequal 10 of 16.
Add bottlenecks and founders with real cases.
Contrast drift with selection: direction, and population size relative to selection strength.
Present sickle-cell trait and malaria as an advantage case with a testable prediction.
Present cystic fibrosis as the unsettled case and teach how to say what is not yet known.
examples: Four survivors from an even mix of alleles A and B: 6 of the 16 equally likely combinations split 2 to 2, so unequal outcomes (10 of 16) are more likely than equal.
Amish colony founded by two members who shared the Ellis-van Creveld allele; prairie chickens fell from about 100 million birds to about 50 in Illinois, with measured loss of variation.

Sickle trait: resistance to malaria; the allele is common where malaria is; as antimalarial treatment spreads the frequency is expected to fall. Cystic fibrosis: about 1 in 25 carriers, advantage hypotheses (cholera, tuberculosis) unsettled, drift possible.

figures.shows: Twenty marbles in a jar, red and blue, redrawn for generations at population sizes 20 and 200.
figures.learnerAction: Run generations and watch which size loses an allele sooner.
figures.placement: Drift in small and large populations

figures.shows: A map of a source population and a small founding colony with allele frequencies drawn as pie slices.
figures.learnerAction: Compare the colony's allele pie with the source's.

questionPlan.sample: A recessive disease allele is at frequency 0.30 in an isolated colony founded by 12 people and 0.01 on the mainland. What is the best first explanation?
questionPlan.answer: A founder effect: a small random sample of the source population
choices: Selection favours the allele on the island
A founder effect: a small random sample of the source population
A higher mutation rate on the island
The mainland measurement is wrong
questionPlan.why: Selection for a disease allele needs evidence of an advantage; a higher mutation rate would not reach 0.30 so fast. A founder sample explains it without extra assumptions.

questionPlan.sample: Two populations start with allele A at 0.5, one of 40 individuals and one of 4,000. Which shows the larger random change in one generation?
questionPlan.answer: The population of 40
choices: The population of 4,000
The population of 40
Both equally
Neither, drift is selection
questionPlan.why: The magnitude of drift per generation is larger when allele copies are few. 'The larger one' mixes up the law of large numbers.

questionPlan.sample: Four survivors are drawn at random from a large population in which alleles A and B are equally common. What is the probability they carry two A and two B?
questionPlan.why: 6 of the 16 equally likely allele combinations split 2 to 2.

questionPlan.sample: Heterozygote advantage is proposed for the sickle allele. Which finding would count against it?
questionPlan.answer: Carrier children in a malaria region get malaria as often and as severely as non-carriers
choices: The allele is common where malaria is common
Carrier children in a malaria region get malaria as often and as severely as non-carriers
Allele frequency falls as malaria is treated
Carriers' infected red cells are cleared quickly
questionPlan.why: The proposal predicts carrier resistance, so equal infection rates contradict it. Higher allele frequency in malaria regions is the pattern the idea explains, not a test.

questionPlan.sample: Carrier mice show less cholera-related diarrhoea than non-carrier mice, but a human study finds carriers indistinguishable from non-carriers. What should you conclude about why cystic fibrosis is common?
questionPlan.answer: The mouse result does not establish a human advantage; selection versus drift is still unsettled
choices: Cholera resistance explains it
The mouse result does not establish a human advantage; selection versus drift is still unsettled
Drift alone explains it
Carriers have no health effects at all
questionPlan.why: A model organism result does not settle a human question. Choosing selection or drift outright goes beyond the evidence.

questionPlan.sample: Prairie chickens fall from about 100 million to about 50 in a state, and DNA from older and newer birds shows lost variation. What event is this?
questionPlan.answer: bottleneck
questionPlan.why: A sharp drop in numbers leaves a small random sample of the alleles.

lessons.title: What a genetic test tells you
lessons.objective: Read a genetic test result: say which question the test was built to answer, what a positive, negative or uncertain result does and does not tell this person, and how to state a risk figure fairly.

concepts.title: Kinds of test
concepts.summary: Targeted single-variant, single-gene, panel, exome or genome sequencing, chromosomal, expression and biochemical tests answer different questions.

concepts.title: What a result means
concepts.summary: A positive result shows a variant, not a diagnosis or a date; a negative result means only that the test found nothing it can detect; some results are uninformative.

concepts.title: Variant classes
concepts.summary: Variants are classed pathogenic, likely pathogenic, of uncertain significance, likely benign or benign, and the class can change as evidence grows.

concepts.title: Validity and utility
concepts.summary: Analytical validity is whether the test detects the variant; clinical validity whether the variant matters for disease; clinical utility whether the result helps care.

misconceptions: A positive result means the person will get the disease. Penetrance is often below 100 percent.
A negative result means no risk. It depends on what is known in the family and on what the test can detect.
A variant of uncertain significance is a mild positive. Most are later reclassified as benign, and care should follow family history meanwhile.
An accurate lab means a useful test. Analytical validity is separate from clinical validity and utility.
A consumer test reads whole genes. Many check only selected variants.
sequence: Lay out the kinds of test and match each to a question.
Read the three outcomes: positive, negative, uncertain.
Give the five variant classes and why they change over time.
Use BRCA numbers to state absolute risk against the general population.
Separate analytical validity, clinical validity and utility.
Close with limits: exome tests miss variants outside exons, and secondary findings arrive unasked.
examples: Lifetime breast cancer: more than 60 percent for women with a harmful BRCA1 or BRCA2 change against about 13 percent in the general population; ovarian cancer 39 to 58 percent (BRCA1) and 13 to 29 percent (BRCA2) against about 1.1 percent.
At 39 to 58 percent, 42 to 61 percent of BRCA1 carriers are not expected to develop ovarian cancer (derived), and the ratio to the general population is roughly 35 to 53 times (derived).
A negative result in a woman whose sister carries a known BRCA1 variant shows she did not inherit it; a negative result in a woman with no known family variant adds nothing beyond family history.

figures.shows: A six-row table of clinical questions beside the test types, shuffled.
figures.learnerAction: Match each question to a test type.

figures.shows: Two 100-person icon arrays, general population and BRCA carriers, for lifetime ovarian cancer, filled to the pack's percentages (1.1 and 39 to 58).
figures.learnerAction: Slide the BRCA1/BRCA2 selector; no answers shown before the learner estimates.

questionPlan.sample: Match each case to the test best suited to it: (1) brother of someone with a known variant; (2) epilepsy of unknown cause that many genes can produce; (3) a child whose single-gene and panel tests have found nothing; (4) a suspected large chromosome deletion; (5) suspected enzyme deficiency from low enzyme activity. Tests: targeted single variant / gene panel / exome or genome sequencing / chromosomal / biochemical.
questionPlan.answer: 1 targeted single variant; 2 gene panel; 3 exome or genome; 4 chromosomal; 5 biochemical
questionPlan.why: Each test type was built for a particular question; the known family variant needs only a targeted look, an unclear picture needs the widest net.

questionPlan.sample: A woman whose sister carries a known harmful BRCA1 change tests negative for that change. What does the result mean?
questionPlan.answer: She did not inherit the family's change and cannot pass it on, though other risks remain
choices: She has no cancer risk
She did not inherit the family's change and cannot pass it on, though other risks remain
The result is inconclusive
She is a carrier with reduced penetrance
questionPlan.why: A negative result that matches a known family variant is clear for that variant. It does not remove all cancer risk. 'No risk' and 'inconclusive' both misread what the lab looked for.

questionPlan.sample: A panel finds a variant of uncertain significance in BRCA2 in a woman with no known family variant. What should guide her care now?
questionPlan.answer: Her family history and other risk factors, not the variant, until it is reclassified
choices: Treat it as a harmful variant
Her family history and other risk factors, not the variant, until it is reclassified
Ignore all risk
Repeat the same test in a month
questionPlan.why: A VUS cannot confirm or rule out a role in disease, and most turn out benign; treating it as pathogenic or as safe both go beyond the evidence.

questionPlan.sample: Which sentence best tells a BRCA1 carrier about her lifetime ovarian cancer risk (39 to 58 percent, against about 1.1 percent)?
questionPlan.answer: Her risk is many times higher than average, but not all carriers develop it
choices: She will develop ovarian cancer
Her risk is many times higher than average, but not all carriers develop it
Her risk is about average
The test cannot give any figure
questionPlan.why: The risk is far above average but below certainty. 'Will develop' ignores that 42 to 61 percent do not; 'about average' ignores the 35-fold or more rise.

questionPlan.sample: A consumer genetic test is analytically accurate for variant X, but the link between X and the disease is weak. Which kind of validity is missing?
questionPlan.answer: Clinical validity
choices: Analytical validity
Clinical validity
Quality control
Clinical utility only
questionPlan.why: Analytical validity is whether the test detects X; clinical validity is whether X is related to the disease; utility is whether the result helps care. Lab standards cover only the first.

lessons.title: Genome scans and risk scores
lessons.objective: Read a genome-wide association result: compute and interpret an odds ratio, explain the strict significance threshold, say why a top SNP need not be causal, and turn a polygenic score into relative and absolute risk without overclaiming.

concepts.title: Genome-wide association study
concepts.summary: Compare allele frequencies at a million or more SNPs between cases and controls; report an odds ratio and a p-value for each.

concepts.title: Significance threshold
concepts.summary: Because so many SNPs are tested, a p-value below 5×10⁻⁸ is required.

concepts.title: Tag SNPs
concepts.summary: An associated SNP may only travel with the causal variant, so fine-mapping is needed.

concepts.title: Polygenic risk score
concepts.summary: A sum over many small-effect variants that ranks relative risk; it gives no baseline or timing and works best in the ancestry it was built on.

misconceptions: The top SNP is the causal variant. It may be tagging the real one through linkage.
p below 0.05 is enough. With a million tests that would flag about 50,000 by chance.
A small odds ratio is useless. Many small effects can add into a useful score.
A polygenic score is a person's chance of disease. It ranks relative risk and says nothing about timing or baseline.
Scores and associations transfer across ancestries. Most data are from European-ancestry people.
sequence: Start with exome and genome sequencing and where the variants come from.
Define a case-control GWAS and the odds ratio with a worked table.
Explain why the threshold is 5×10⁻⁸ and read a Manhattan plot.
Say why an associated SNP is not necessarily causal (tagging; fine-mapping).
Move to polygenic scores: relative versus absolute risk, the 22-year-old and 98-year-old.
End with limits: ancestry, small effect sizes, and what AUC values imply.
examples: Allele T: 600 in cases and 500 in controls; allele C: 400 in cases and 500 in controls. Odds ratio (600/500)/(400/500) = 1.5 (invented counts, pack formula).
Testing 1,000,000 SNPs at p 0.05 gives about 50,000 chance hits; at 5×10⁻⁸ about 0.05 (derived).
AUC 0.64 for a coronary disease score from genes alone and about 0.80 once age and sex are added (pack, Wikipedia).

figures.shows: A Manhattan plot (22 chromosome strips, minus log10 p on the y-axis, a line at 7.3 for 5×10⁻⁸, one tall stack on one chromosome).
figures.learnerAction: Tap points above and below the line; no p-values shown before the learner tries.

figures.shows: Two equal polygenic scores for coronary disease for a 22-year-old and a 98-year-old with separate baseline-risk bars hidden until the learner commits.
figures.learnerAction: Estimate which has the higher lifetime risk before revealing the baselines.

questionPlan.sample: In cases, 600 carry allele T and 400 carry allele C. In controls, 500 carry T and 500 carry C. What is the odds ratio for allele T, (A/B)/(X/Y) with A and X the cases' T and C counts and B and Y the controls'?
A GWAS tests one million SNPs. Why do the authors demand p below 5×10⁻⁸ and not 0.05?
questionPlan.answer: With a million tests, 0.05 would flag about 50,000 SNPs by chance alone
choices: Large effects need a stricter test
With a million tests, 0.05 would flag about 50,000 SNPs by chance alone
Small studies need stricter tests
Odds ratios below 1.33 cannot be significant
questionPlan.why: The reason is multiple testing; it is not about effect size or sample size. The threshold is not arbitrary strictness: at 5×10⁻⁸ chance would flag about 0.05 SNPs.

questionPlan.sample: The tallest stack in a Manhattan plot sits on one chromosome, far above the line. What is the best reading?
questionPlan.answer: A region is associated; the top SNP may only tag the causal variant nearby, so fine-mapping is needed
choices: The top SNP is the causal variant
A region is associated; the top SNP may only tag the causal variant nearby, so fine-mapping is needed
The stack is probably a mistake
The disease is caused by that whole chromosome
questionPlan.why: Linkage disequilibrium means nearby variants travel together, so the top SNP is not necessarily causal. 'The gene is that SNP' and 'ignore the stack' both skip that step.

questionPlan.sample: A 22-year-old and a 98-year-old have the same high polygenic score for coronary disease. Which statement is right?
questionPlan.answer: They have the same relative standing but different lifetime risks
choices: They have the same lifetime risk
They have the same relative standing but different lifetime risks
The older person certainly has the disease
The score is meaningless
questionPlan.why: A polygenic score only ranks relative risk; it carries no baseline or timeframe. The same score does not give the same absolute risk.

questionPlan.sample: A coronary disease score reaches AUC 0.64 from genetic information alone and about 0.80 once age and sex are included. What is the fair summary?
questionPlan.answer: The score alone predicts weakly; with age and sex it does much better
choices: The genetic score is enough to diagnose
The score alone predicts weakly; with age and sex it does much better
Age and sex add nothing
AUC cannot compare scores
questionPlan.why: The pack gives only that larger AUC means better prediction. Calling the genetic score diagnostic goes further than a value of 0.64 allows, and age and sex add real information.

lessons.title: Editing a genome
lessons.objective: Choose and critique a genome-editing approach for a stated goal: which repair route gives a knockout and which a precise change, what a guide RNA must match, what can go wrong, and what changes when the edited cells are germline.

concepts.title: Cas9 and guide RNA
concepts.summary: A guide RNA matches a target sequence and Cas9 cuts the DNA there; Cas9 also needs a short adjacent site (PAM, NGG) that occurs every 8 to 12 base pairs.

concepts.title: Two repair routes
concepts.summary: End joining leaves random insertions or deletions (knockout); homology-directed repair with a supplied template inserts a chosen sequence (knock-in); base editors change single bases without a template.

concepts.title: What can go wrong
concepts.summary: Off-target cuts, immune response to bacterial parts, vector capacity and mosaicism limit use.

concepts.title: Somatic and germline edits
concepts.summary: Edits in body cells stay in one person; edits in eggs, sperm or embryos can be inherited and are currently illegal in the United States and many countries.

misconceptions: CRISPR repairs the gene by itself. The cell's repair machinery decides the outcome, so a template is needed for a precise change.
Every cell ends up with the same edit. Edits can be mosaic.
An edit in blood stem cells is inherited. Somatic edits are not passed on.
The 20-base match is the same as the PAM. The PAM occurs every 8 to 12 base pairs; the guide gives the specificity.
Editing is still only in animals. The pack's sources show approvals; check the source's date.
sequence: Start from the bacterial immune system and the idea of a programmable cut.
Describe the guide RNA, Cas9 and PAM, and why a 20-base match is specific.
Contrast end joining (knockout) with homology-directed repair and base editing.
List the failure modes: off-target, immune response, vector size, mosaicism.
Look at a real therapy: edited blood stem cells for sickle-cell disease and beta thalassemia.
Separate somatic from germline and say why the law and the field treat them differently.
examples: Goal: switch off a gene. Route: a cut repaired by end joining usually leaves insertions or deletions that disrupt it.
Goal: make one C-to-T change in a point mutation. Route: a base editor, with no donor template.
A 2018 embryo edit left some functional copies alongside disabled ones (mosaicism), so the children were not uniformly edited.

figures.shows: A DNA strand with a 20-base guide match, the NGG site, the cut, and three branches for repair (end joining, template, base editor) shown as switchable views.
figures.learnerAction: Pick a goal and drag it onto the repair route that serves it; outcomes hidden until commit.

figures.shows: Somatic and germline columns with rows for who carries the edit, whether it can be inherited, and the legal position.
figures.learnerAction: Fill the rows.

questionPlan.sample: Match each goal to the route: (1) switch off a gene; (2) insert a chosen sequence at an exact site; (3) change one C to a T. Routes: cut and end joining / cut with a repair template / base editor.
questionPlan.answer: 1 cut and end joining; 2 cut with a repair template; 3 base editor
questionPlan.why: End joining leaves random insertions or deletions, which disrupt a gene; a template guides repair to a chosen sequence; a base editor changes single bases without a donor.

questionPlan.sample: A treated cell line has the intended edit and also a small deletion at another site that partly matches the guide. What is the best description?
questionPlan.answer: An off-target cut
choices: A delivery failure
An off-target cut
Mosaicism
A normal repair outcome
questionPlan.why: Off-target cuts occur where the guide partly matches. Delivery failure and mosaicism describe other problems, and a random mutation would not match the guide.

questionPlan.sample: A patient's blood stem cells are edited to treat sickle-cell disease. Will her future children inherit the edit?
questionPlan.answer: No: the edit is in body cells, not eggs or sperm
choices: Yes, all of them
No: the edit is in body cells, not eggs or sperm
Only her daughters
Only if she is a carrier
questionPlan.why: Edits limited to somatic cells (here blood stem cells) are not passed on. 'Yes' treats any edit as hereditary; 'only daughters' invents a mechanism.

questionPlan.sample: Why is it hard to deliver the full Cas9 gene in a small viral vector?
questionPlan.answer: The vector's capacity is small and Cas9 is large, and bacterial parts can trigger an immune response
choices: Viruses cannot enter cells
The vector's capacity is small and Cas9 is large, and bacterial parts can trigger an immune response
Cas9 is too small to be useful
Guides cannot be packaged
questionPlan.why: The pack names capacity and immune response; 'viruses cannot enter cells' and 'Cas9 is too small' are wrong.

questionPlan.sample: A report on an edited embryo says half the sampled cells carry the edit. Why does this matter?
questionPlan.answer: Not every cell carries the edit, so one sample cannot show how the individual is edited
choices: It does not matter, editing is uniform
Not every cell carries the edit, so one sample cannot show how the individual is edited
It shows the edit failed
It shows the edit is inherited
questionPlan.why: Mosaicism means different cells hold different versions, so a sample misleads.

questionPlan.sample: A health site says genome editing is used only in labs and animals, yet another source reports an approved CRISPR therapy. What is the best response?
questionPlan.answer: Check the dates: the first page's statement may predate the approvals
choices: Trust the health site
Check the dates: the first page's statement may predate the approvals
Trust the newer source without checking it
Assume both are wrong
questionPlan.why: Two sources can both be right at different dates. Neither 'one is wrong' nor 'average them' fits.

lessons.title: Weighing epigenetic claims
lessons.objective: Say what epigenetic marks are and do, separate what is well supported (cell identity, X inactivation, imprinting, change with age) from what is contested (transgenerational inheritance in humans), and judge a claim by which generation is first free of direct exposure.

concepts.title: Epigenetic marks
concepts.summary: DNA methylation and histone modification change how a gene is expressed without changing the DNA sequence, and can be copied when cells divide.

concepts.title: X inactivation and imprinting
concepts.summary: One X is silenced at random in each cell of a female; imprinted genes are expressed according to which parent supplied them.

concepts.title: Reprogramming
concepts.summary: Most marks are erased after fertilization and in germ-cell precursors, so inheritance across generations needs marks to escape both.

concepts.title: First generation free of exposure
concepts.summary: Proposed criteria require an effect in generations with no direct exposure: F2 or later for fathers, F3 or later for pregnant mothers.

misconceptions: Epigenetic means inherited. Most marks are reset between generations.
Any lifestyle change rewrites the epigenome and passes to children. That claim is not established in humans.
Epigenetic marks are permanent. They are reversible and are not selected in themselves.
A grandchild effect after famine in pregnancy proves transgenerational epigenetic inheritance. The fetus and its germ cells were exposed.
Epigenetics lets the mind control the genes. The pack warns against that pseudoscience.
sequence: Define epigenetics, DNA methylation and histone modification.
Show well-supported effects: cell identity, tortoiseshell cats and X inactivation, imprinting (Angelman and Prader-Willi), epigenetic differences growing in identical twins.
Explain reprogramming and why it makes inheritance hard.
Give the criteria and use the Dutch hunger winter as the test case (fetal programming).
Cover the 2026 review of human trauma studies as the cautionary case.
Recap as three questions: what is the mark, what is the evidence, which generation is first unexposed?
examples: Tortoiseshell cats are heterozygous females: patches in which different X chromosomes were inactivated.
The same 15q deletion causes Angelman or Prader-Willi syndrome depending on which parent supplied it.

A mother exposed while pregnant: F0 mother, F1 fetus, F2 the fetus's germ cells (exposed in utero); the first generation free of exposure is F3, so an F2 effect does not meet the criterion (derived from the pack's F3 rule and fetal programming account).

figures.shows: Three generation tracks, exposed father and exposed pregnant mother, with germ cells shown in each generation and shading for direct exposure.
