figures.learnerAction: Tap the first generation that is not directly exposed in each track.

figures.shows: A female cell with two X chromosomes, one coloured and one grey, and a division sequence showing the same X inactive in all descendants.
figures.learnerAction: Run divisions and watch the pattern appear as patches.

questionPlan.sample: Pregnant women are exposed to famine; their grandchildren show raised disease risk. Does that alone demonstrate transgenerational epigenetic inheritance?
questionPlan.answer: Not by the proposed criteria: for an exposed pregnant mother the first generation with no direct exposure is the great-grandchildren
choices: Yes, the grandchildren were never exposed
Not by the proposed criteria: for an exposed pregnant mother the first generation with no direct exposure is the great-grandchildren
No, because epigenetic effects cannot occur in humans
Yes, but only for fathers
questionPlan.why: The fetus (F1) and its germ cells (which become F2) are exposed in utero; the criteria call for effects at F3 or later for maternal exposure. 'Yes, grandchildren are unexposed' misses that.

questionPlan.sample: Which statement about DNA methylation is best supported?
questionPlan.answer: A methylated gene is turned down or off, and the pattern can be copied through cell divisions
choices: Methylation changes the DNA sequence
A methylated gene is turned down or off, and the pattern can be copied through cell divisions
Methylation marks always pass to children
Methylation permanently locks a gene off
questionPlan.why: Methyl groups on a gene silence it. Marks are modifications on top of the sequence rather than changes to it, and most marks are reset between generations.

questionPlan.sample: The same deletion on chromosome 15 gives Angelman syndrome when inherited from the mother and Prader-Willi when from the father. What explains it?
questionPlan.answer: Genomic imprinting: the parent of origin determines which copy is expressed
choices: Two different mutations
Genomic imprinting: the parent of origin determines which copy is expressed
Random chance
A diet effect
questionPlan.why: The deletion is the same, so two different mutations is wrong. Chance and environment do not follow the parent.

questionPlan.sample: Male tortoiseshell cats are very rare; female ones are common. Why?
questionPlan.answer: Tortoiseshell needs two different X chromosomes active in different patches, which requires two X chromosomes
choices: Males lack the orange gene
Tortoiseshell needs two different X chromosomes active in different patches, which requires two X chromosomes
Males inactivate both X chromosomes
Tortoiseshell is an environmental trait
questionPlan.why: X inactivation silences one X at random in each cell of a female heterozygote, giving patches; a male has one X and the Y.

questionPlan.sample: A wellness article says that a meditation habit rewrites your epigenome and your children will inherit the change. Which part is weakest?
questionPlan.answer: That children will inherit it: marks are largely reset in germ cells and human evidence is weak
choices: That the epigenome can change at all
That children will inherit it: marks are largely reset in germ cells and human evidence is weak
That genes can be switched on and off
That methylation exists
questionPlan.why: Marks can change with environment, so the first part is plausible; the inheritance claim runs against reprogramming and the human evidence.

questionPlan.sample: Older identical twins show larger methylation differences than young twins. What does this best support?
questionPlan.answer: Environment and time alter the epigenome even when the DNA sequence is the same
choices: Their DNA sequences differ more with age
Environment and time alter the epigenome even when the DNA sequence is the same
Epigenetic marks are fixed at birth
Twins are not identical
questionPlan.why: Identical twins share their sequence, so the differences are not sequence changes. Calling it a DNA difference or a genetic failure misses the point.

courseCheck: A mixed check across the course. Translate a short coding sequence and classify a change in it. Predict lac operon expression for a mutant in two conditions, including a partial diploid. Infer a parent's genotype from a test-cross count and name the ratio in an epistasis cross. Compute a recombination frequency, checking the parents' arrangement. Rule modes of inheritance in or out on a pedigree and chain a carrier probability. Separate penetrance, expressivity and heritability in a case. Estimate carriers from a disease incidence and read a heterozygote deficit. Choose between drift, founder effect and selection for an allele pattern. Interpret a negative, positive and uncertain test result and state a risk in absolute terms. Compute an odds ratio and say why a top SNP may not be causal. Match goals to editing routes and say whether an edit is heritable. Find the first unexposed generation in a claimed epigenetic inheritance.
platformNeeds: A codon-table and reading-frame explorer: a strip of mRNA, a movable frame and the table's amino acids appearing as the frame moves. Fallback: svg_figure with the three frames drawn as fixed views.
A pedigree figure with standard symbols, tap-to-mark carriers and a probability field. Fallback: three fixed svg_figure pedigrees (A, B, C in lesson 7) with a mode checklist.
A Manhattan plot with a threshold line and tappable points. Fallback: svg_figure with fixed points and the line at 7.3 (minus log10 of 5×10⁻⁸).
A recombination bench: test-cross counts with live recombination frequency and map distance. Fallback: the table figure with counts given.
Question kind `sort` is used in lessons 1, 4, 8, 11 and 13 and `order_sequence` in lessons 2 and 6; both exist today.
unverified: RNA's use of uracil in place of thymine and the template-versus-coding-strand rule are not stated as rules in the pack; lesson 2 follows the NCBI convention (code table written with T for U) and gives learners mRNA with U.
Every codon translation, the single-base routes between Glu and Val, and the frameshift results are derived from the NCBI table in the pack and were checked by script, not stated by any source.
Lac operon partial-diploid outcomes (lesson 3) are derived from the pack's statements that the operator mutation acts only in cis and the repressor gene acts in trans; no source works the cases.
The 25 percent normal-dimer figure (lesson 4) assumes random subunit pairing, which the pack does not state.
Pink x pink giving 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white follows from incomplete dominance and the 1:2:1 genotype ratio of two heterozygotes; the pack states each part separately.
Reciprocal-cross results for the white gene are in a figure the pack lacks; lesson 5 derives them from the hemizygous rule.
The pack has no chi-square procedure (deferred to the book's labs) and the Hardy-Weinberg chi-square example is garbled, so the course asks what the test is for, not how to run it.
Three-point crosses and interference are not in the pack.
The pack has no selection coefficient arithmetic or worked selection example; lesson 10 is qualitative apart from the four-bacteria probability.
The AUC baseline for a useless score (0.5) is not stated in the pack and is not used.
MedlinePlus says exons are about 1 percent of the genome; NHGRI's cost page says about 1.5 percent. The course says 'about 1 percent' and does not use the NHGRI figure.

The pack gives no efficacy or safety numbers for any gene-editing therapy; Casgevy facts come from one Wikipedia page, which does not say whether the cells are edited inside or outside the body, so lesson 13 does not say.
MedlinePlus says the BRCA1 absolute risk of breast cancer is 60 to 80 percent (via NHGRI); NCI says more than 60 percent. The course uses NCI's figures.

The MedlinePlus height page says 'about 80 percent of height is determined by' inherited variants, which reads as a causal share; its own heritability page warns against that reading. Lesson 8 uses the contradiction as a teaching case.
Pedigrees A, B and C and the invented counts (test cross 38/44/9/9, 412/388/98/102, Hardy-Weinberg 200/80/40, Labrador 88/33/39, odds ratio table) are invented teaching cases and must be labelled so.
